messages.body_plain:
Hi,
Could you please share the code for reproducing the image from the Github README.md file?
I'd like to run a similar analysis on several samples from a microbiome study.
I looked at the dev package but there still doesn't seem to be an easy way of handling OTU tables with metacoder, or am I missing something here?

Thanks in advance!
Roey

messages.body_plain:
Hello Roey,

The code to produce that figure can be found here:

https://grunwaldlab.github.io/metacoder_documentation/publication--05--16s_human_microbiome.html

In regards to storing OTU tables, currently you would store that information in the `taxon_data` or `obs_data` tables in the `taxmap` objects (the main object used to store information in `metacoder`). Typically the counts for each OTU would stored in the `obs_data` table and the counts summed per taxon in the `taxon_data` table. Samples would be columns for both. This works, but it would be better if there was dedicated tables for this information. We are currently working on the taxa package (https://github.com/ropensci/taxa) to store this make the `taxmap` object more flexible. Once this is on CRAN, I will work of making a function that will make the heat tree matrix visualization easier, but for now you can adapt the code in the tutorial I linked above. Hope this helps and let me know if you have questions.

-Zach

messages.subject: Re: producing trees with the say layout
messages.subject_clean: producing trees with the say layout
messages.body_plain:
Hello Dan,

Good question. I assume each sample has different a different set of taxa in the trees? There is currently no way of forcing a given taxon to be in a given place.  If the taxa are different, the placement will be different. One way you might be able to get around this would be to make sure all trees you want to have the same layout have the same set of taxa. You could include all taxa that appear in any of the samples for example. For a given sample, you can then use color/size to show that these taxa are absent (e.g. `node_color = ifelse(my_taxon_counts ==  0, "grey", my_stat_of_interest)`). I think you could also make the nodes/edges invisible by setting their color to `NA`, but they would still take up space in the layout, so that might not work for well for all data. Thats about all I can think of. At the moment, I cannot think of any easy change I could make to the package that would address this better, but I will keep it in mind. Hope this helps,

-Zach

messages.subject: Re: Ratio trees
messages.body_plain:
Hi Dan,

I am glad it worked out!

That graph used read depth from the human microbiome project. The input was an abundance matrix. There was also a separate table that had which samples were in each treatment. If you are starting from FASTA files, the process would be different at the start at least and its hard for me to say what to do without knowing more about how your data is formatted.

The basic process for figure 5 was as follows:

* Get an abundance (number of reads/sequences) matrix of samples vs OTUs that has taxonomic classifications for OTUs.
* Parse using `parse_taxonomy_table`. This will put the abundance matrix in the `obs_data`.
* Calculate the abundance of each taxon for each sample and put that in `taxa_data`.
* Divide each column by the the total number of reads to get proportions
* For each pair of treatments you want to compare, calculate the difference in median proportions for each taxon. I find it useful to do this in a function that makes each subplot so you dont have to add columns for every pairwise comparison to a single table, which would be hard to name columns and parse.  You can also use a wilcox rank sum test here and set any difference to 0 that is not significant.
* Use color to plot the difference in median proportions for each pair of treatments. I log transformed it so that it is centered on zero.

You can see the code for figure 5 here:

https://grunwaldlab.github.io/metacoder_documentation/publication--05--16s_human_microbiome.html

Do you have an abundance matrix?
